summary:
Visitors to Corsica stand under the framework of French national law. Identity-document rules, criminal procedure, anti-discrimination law and marriage law are uniform across metropolitan and overseas regions, and the risks documented for trans travellers in France apply unchanged in this region.

No findings specific to Corsica appear in the surviving sources. The national mechanisms the sources document concern detention and the border, and there is no evidence that Corsican establishments depart from the national pattern.

Placement of trans detainees follows no statutory safeguard. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, and in practice placement is decided by the sex inscribed on a person's identity documents. As a result trans women are typically held in men's facilities.

The scale of that practice was small but recorded: as of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight French establishments, the majority of them at the Fleury-Mérogis men's prison near Paris.

French law does not automatically recognise a trans detainee's foreign legal gender for placement purposes. The BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 despite a passport listing her as female, where she met shouts of "We don't want any women here".

The same feature documents inconsistent access to treatment for trans detainees and a symbolic damages award of 2,000 euros over detention conditions. It records the justice minister being pressed to amend Article D248.

The Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion dated 25 May 2021 on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty. The opinion builds on referrals received since 2010 and on a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners, and it covers all places of deprivation of liberty.

Inspections cited in the 2021 opinion include the prisons of Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women. The opinion documents discrimination, stigmatisation and blind spots in health and social care, and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion these detainees face.

The opinion references law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers, and the "racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination" referents appointed in French detention settings since 2018. Across the prisons it inspected, the CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of the rights of trans detainees.
tangentialFactors:
The border is the second documented risk setting for trans travellers to France. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes French border police at the airport questioning her identity documents in public for ten minutes in front of other travellers, an episode she frames as routine humiliation. Document friction of this kind is not Corsica-specific; it is the documented French entry-point experience.

The Défenseur des droits has issued a framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from its case files and from association testimony. The decision cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and it sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013. CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect. Marriage recognition is settled law rather than an open question in Corsica.

Prison placement by identity-document sex is the practice most likely to reach a visitor, since arrest or custody during a trip places a trans person directly inside the mechanism the CGLPL has criticised. Isolation arrangements and strip-search exposure, recorded by the CGLPL as violations, are custodial conditions that a foreign national held in a Corsican or mainland French facility would face.
localsOnly:
The placement rule has a named legal anchor that Corsican residents can cite: Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which separates establishments by sex. The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 is a binding, citable instrument in France, and its referrals process has accepted complaints from trans detainees since 2010.

French law recognises legal gender recognition, referenced through law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers. That law is the one the CGLPL relies on when pressing for placement reform.

Since 2018 French detention establishments have appointed "racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination" referents. These are the internal channels through which a trans detainee in a Corsican or mainland facility would raise a complaint about placement or isolation.

The Défenseur des droits framework decision on trans rights provides official guidance for service providers, and its case-file evidence draws on associations' testimony. Residents facing discrimination in accommodation or services have an established national body to approach, and the EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey figures give a documented measure of identity-related discrimination against trans people in France.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the CGLPL has inspected any specific Corsican prison is not addressed in the sources provided, and no inspection of a Corsican establishment is documented here. The CGLPL's findings cover the prisons it inspected, namely Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses, so the pattern is stated as national without evidence about individual Corsican facilities.

Whether Article D248 has been amended since the 2018 calls on the justice minister to do so is unresolved in the sources available. The 2021 CGLPL opinion continues to document placement by birth sex as a live violation, which indicates the practice persisted, but no source confirms the current text of the article.

The number of trans detainees recorded, 13 across eight establishments as of 1 November 2016, is a dated snapshot and not a current figure. Present-day detention numbers for trans people in France are not sourced.

French border authorities' current document-verification policy for trans travellers is not documented in the inventory; the 2017 StreetPress account is a single traveller's experience rather than a stated official procedure.
